noticias.titulo: The Gambia election: Can the next president deliver on a decade of promise
noticias.resumen: Gambians head to the polls amid economic hardship and unfulfilled promises of reform and justice.
noticias.texto:
The Gambia election: Can the next president deliver on a decade of promise
Gambians head to the polls amid economic hardship and unfulfilled promises of reform and justice.
Banjul, The Gambia – As Gambians prepare to vote on December 5, unemployment, rising living costs, unreliable public services and delayed justice are testing the country’s democratic transition. Nearly a decade after Yahya Jammeh’s departure, voters are asking whether the next president can deliver the change they were promised.
For Sosseh Jagne, the election is about more than who occupies the State House. It is about whether the next government can create conditions in which Gambians can earn a living.
Jagne established Ya Anna’s Catering in 2020 and expanded it into a restaurant in early 2025. But frequent electricity outages have disrupted her business, affecting food preparation, refrigeration and customer service. Between August and October, she said, power cuts sometimes lasted 19 hours or longer.
She estimates that spoiled food cost her more than 40,000 Gambian dalasis ($532). She has also stopped selling homemade iced juices because she cannot guarantee they will remain properly chilled.
“Electricity is not a luxury; it is a necessity for people’s everyday lives and, especially, for businesses that depend on it to operate,” she told Al Jazeera.
Her experience reflects the pressures facing households and businesses as President Adama Barrow seeks a third term. He is one of eight candidates in the December 5 election, according to the Independent Electoral Commission. Barrow came to power in 2017 after defeating Jammeh, who ruled the country for 22 years.
The cost of survival
For many young Gambians, the central question is where they can find work.
The 2025 Gambia Labour Force Survey puts overall unemployment at 8.3 percent, up from 7.6 percent in 2022–23. Among people aged 15 to 35, unemployment stands at 11.5 percent. The survey also found that 41.3 percent of young people in that age group were neither employed nor in education or training.
For 26-year-old Maram Mendy, a graduate of the University of The Gambia, finding a job has become increasingly discouraging. Her parents sacrificed to finance her education, making her inability to find work particularly difficult.
“I’m now fed up with looking for a job,” she told Al Jazeera.
She said employers frequently demand previous experience, leaving graduates caught in a cycle: They cannot get a job without experience, but cannot gain experience without employment.
For 28-year-old Buba Sanneh, unemployed since graduating in 2023, the frustration has prompted thoughts of travelling to Europe through irregular migration, commonly known as the backway.
For Hakeem Touray, the search for opportunities abroad has already cost his family dearly. His elder brother, Bob, was 27 when he attempted the journey to Europe in 2021. He died trying to cross the Mediterranean Sea.
Hakeem said the loss highlighted the consequences of unemployment, poverty and limited opportunities at home.
The risks are reflected in figures cited by UN Special Rapporteur Morris Tidball-Binz, following his visit to The Gambia in October 2026. In his end-of-mission statement, he said independent sources had reported that 1,603 Gambians died attempting irregular migration in 2024 and 893 in 2025, most of them at sea. Separately, the International Organization for Migration had recorded at least 408 Gambians missing along migration routes since 2014.
For families, these are not simply statistics but lives lost and loved ones whose fate remains uncertain.
Living costs and basic services
Economic hardship extends beyond unemployment. According to figures published by the Gambia Bureau of Statistics, 53.4 percent of the population – about 1.1 million people – lived below the national poverty line in 2020. The rate was particularly high in rural areas, at about 76 percent, compared with 34 percent in urban areas.
At Bakoteh Market, 38-year-old vegetable seller Fatoumatta Jawara said rising prices have made supporting her family increasingly difficult. She also wants affordable healthcare to become a priority.
“Survival is becoming harder with each passing day. We need a president who will improve our lives for the better,” she told Al Jazeera.
Nearby, 22-year-old Isatou Ceesay, a mother of two, said she had grown tired of politicians’ promises.
“All they do is promise, and after the election you don’t hear from them again. We are tired of their endless promises,” she said.
Security is another concern, particularly in communities near Senegal’s Casamance region. Instability in the neighbouring region has raised concerns about the safety of border communities and the livelihoods that depend on cross-border movement.
The unfinished promise of justice
For families affected by abuses under Jammeh, the 2017 change of government brought hopes of accountability. Nearly a decade later, many are still waiting.
Sainabou Camara Lowe was 17 when security forces violently suppressed student demonstrations in April 2000, leaving more than a dozen students dead. She survived, but sustained a spinal injury that required two operations.
Now 43 and widowed, she raises five children while struggling with limited mobility. Although she received about 900,000 dalasis ($11,970) through the reparations process, she said the payment had done little to ease her family’s hardship.
“We are forgotten as victims and continue to wallow in pain and poverty,” she told Al Jazeera.
Kebba Jome, national coordinator of the Gambia Centre for Victims of Human Rights Violations, said fewer than 25 percent of the 263 recommendations made by the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission had been fully implemented.
A special tribunal to prosecute alleged crimes committed under Jammeh is expected to begin hearings early next year, Jome said. He argued that the next president would have a responsibility to ensure the accountability process moves forward.
For Muhammed and Fatoumatta Sandeng, the children of opposition activist Ebrima Solo Sandeng, justice remains central to the promises made after Jammeh’s departure. Their father died in state custody in April 2016 after being tortured, according to the findings of the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission.
They want the next administration to implement the commission’s recommendations and ensure those responsible for abuses are brought to justice.
“Victims have been waiting, victims are dying,” Fatoumatta said. “Justice is long overdue.”
Competing promises, familiar challenges
These demands come against a backdrop of unfinished political reform. A central pledge of the post-Jammeh transition, replacing the 1997 Constitution, remains unfulfilled.
The 2020 Draft Constitution, drawn up after a public review process, proposed a two-term limit for presidents, among other institutional changes. It failed to secure the required two-thirds majority in the National Assembly in September 2020. Disagreements over the draft included whether Barrow’s first term should count towards the proposed limit. Barrow blamed opposition resistance for its failure and has said he would revisit constitutional reform if re-elected.
His main challenger, Ousainou Darboe, leader of the United Democratic Party (UDP), has pledged to reintroduce the 2020 draft constitution within his first 100 days in office. His party’s 2026 manifesto also commits him to serving one five-year term.
The manifesto sets out proposals for institutional and security-sector reform, reducing the budget of the Office of the President, tackling public debt and improving the delivery of services, including healthcare, education, electricity and water.
Other candidates include Talib Ahmed Bensouda, the former mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and independent candidate Almameh Gibba, who has said he would facilitate Jammeh’s return if elected.
Former Vice President Isatou Touray is seeking to become the country’s first woman president. Campaigning under the symbol of a broom, she has promised a new constitution and improvements in living conditions.
Political scientist Essa Njie said the election would be shaped by economic conditions, candidates’ personalities and party loyalty. While unemployment, the cost of living and corruption are important concerns, he said, some voters would also make their choices along ethnic, religious and political lines.
The next administration will face the challenge of turning campaign commitments into reforms amid institutional constraints and competing political interests.
A vote for a different future?
For many Gambians, December 5 is about whether the next five years will bring tangible improvements to everyday life.
Jagne wants reliable electricity to keep her business running, Mendy wants an opportunity to enter the workforce, and Sanneh wants a future that does not require risking his life on the backway. Market sellers want to feed their children and afford healthcare. Families of victims want accountability and the assurance that their loved ones have not been forgotten.
Nearly a decade after Jammeh’s departure, these expectations remain central to The Gambia’s democratic journey. Whoever wins will inherit not only the responsibility of governing the country but also the burden of promises that remain unfulfilled.
For Hakeem Touray, whose brother died trying to reach Europe, the stakes are particularly personal.
“Our young people are not necessarily running away from The Gambia; many are running away from hopelessness,” he told Al Jazeera.

noticias.titulo: UK warns companies of potential Russian sabotage threat
noticias.resumen: Britain's Defence Ministry and security service warn of the threat in unusual public announcement.
noticias.texto:
UK warns companies of potential Russian sabotage threat
Britain’s Defence Ministry and the country’s security service warn of the threat in an unusual public announcement.
Britain’s Defence Ministry and the country’s security service, known as MI5, are warning companies that support Ukraine’s military that they may face attempted sabotage from Russia.
“If your organisation supports military procurement or supplies equipment to Ukraine’s armed forces, it could be a target,” the Ministry of Defence and the National Protective Security Authority said in an unusual public announcement on Tuesday.
“This activity is typically characterised by the use of proxy actors employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson,” the warning said, urging companies to take action against security threats posed by what they described as operatives acting for Russia.
‘No plans to attack the UK’
Russia’s embassy in London denied such claims in a statement and said: “Russia has no plans, reasons or intentions to attack the UK.”
It also accused Ukraine of carrying out sabotage to “put the blame on Russia and extort more money from western governments”, something Kyiv has repeatedly denied.
Since the Ukraine war started and Britain became one of Kyiv’s key supporters, London has accused Russia of being behind a number of spying and sabotage plots.
Last year, three British men were convicted for an arson attack on a warehouse storing Starlink satellite equipment bound for Ukraine, which prosecutors said was carried out by Russian military intelligence agents.
In September, a man was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service after alleged contact with Russian military spies.
On Sunday, Estonia said it would close all its border crossing points with Russia following a suspected sabotage attack on an Estonian defence company, while last week the Norwegian security service said it expected Russian intelligence to carry out sabotage attacks in Norway in the coming year.
UK closed-door security briefings
Britain’s Ministry of Defence said it was holding closed-door security briefings with leaders from the critical national infrastructure and defence sectors over the next two days to advise on security.
“Recent sabotage attempts right across Europe demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face,” Security Minister Dan Jarvis said.
“It’s truly shameful that actors are seeking to disrupt our way of life and that of our allies, especially targeting organisations doing vital work in support of Ukraine.”

noticias.titulo: Asia’s stock markets dive as doubts swirl over AI boom
noticias.resumen: Markets fall sharply in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan in latest tech-led sell-off.
noticias.texto:
Asia’s stock markets dive as doubts swirl over AI boom
Markets fall sharply in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan in latest tech-led sell-off.
Asian stock markets have fallen sharply as doubts continue to swirl over the AI boom, reversing a rally sparked by Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia.
Taiwan’s stock market led the sell-off, with the benchmark Taiex plunging as much as 7.9 percent in morning trading.
South Korea’s Kospi fell more than 6 percent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 3.6 percent.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index bucked the trend, rising by as much as 1.3 percent.
Tech stocks linked to AI trade suffered some of the steepest losses.
In Japan, Tokyo Electron, a leading manufacturer of semiconductor fabrication equipment, dived 13.5 percent, while Advantest, a producer of chip testing equipment, plunged 14.5 percent.
South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the top two global memory chip makers, sank 9.1 percent and 9.9 percent, respectively.
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s biggest contract chip maker, and Taiwanese Apple supplier Foxconn both dropped more than 9 percent.
AI headwinds
The retreat comes after Asian markets surged on Tuesday following Huang’s surprise reinstatement at the helm of chip giant Nvidia after an intervention by US President Donald Trump.
Nvidia’s reappointment of Huang, who resigned amid claims he was romantically involved with a woman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, sent the chip giant’s New York-listed shares 31.5 percent higher on Monday, the largest single-day gain in US stock market history.
Wall Street saw modest losses on Tuesday after the previous session’s buying spree, with the S&P 500 falling 0.5 percent and the Nasdaq composite down 1.5 percent.
Markets have seen wild swings over the past month amid the Nvidia scandal and expectations that Democrats in Washington, DC, will push for greater regulation of AI following their sweeping victories in the US midterm elections.
Those headwinds have added to existing concerns that tech firms may not be able to sustain their multi-trillion-dollar investments underpinning the AI boom.
Big Tech’s debt-fuelled splurge has stirred intense debate about whether it is investing in a future gold mine or a massive stock market bubble.
Global AI-related investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

noticias.titulo: Kilmar Abrego Garcia self-deports to Spain after lengthy US legal battle
noticias.resumen: US Senator Chris Van Hollen hails Kilmar Abrego Garcia's safe departure to Spain as a 'free man'.
noticias.texto:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia self-deports to Spain after lengthy US legal battle
US Senator Chris Van Hollen hails Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s safe departure to Spain as a ‘free man’.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was wrongfully deported to El Salvador last year as part of United States President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has self-deported to Spain.
Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national, voluntarily departed on Tuesday after months of legal opposition to a second deportation, this time to one of various African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.
A judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport on Tuesday, The Associated Press reported, citing a source familiar with the matter.
US Senator Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia while pressing for his release from Salvadoran mega-prison CECOT, said Abrego Garcia is “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man”.
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen, who is vying for Senate majority leader, said in a statement posted on X.
Salvadoran prison
Abrego Garcia, 31, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison notorious for abusive conditions and alleged use of torture.
The Trump administration, at the time, described Abrego Garcia’s deportation as an “administrative error”. However, the administration initially refused to seek his return, arguing that Abrego Garcia was a member of the MS-13 gang despite having no criminal record at the time of his removal.
In June 2025, the Trump administration brought him back after facing public pressure and a court order, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee.
The Tennessee case was dismissed by a federal judge in May, though the government appealed it in August.
Abrego Garcia had said that if he must be deported, he would prefer to be sent to Costa Rica, but Todd Lyons, the former acting director of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said that deporting him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States” in a March 2026 memo.
Lyons wrote that Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the US has spent government resources and political capital negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals.
The memo came despite a US agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.
Abrego Garcia has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager.
In 2019, an immigration judge issued an order saying that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family.
The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, but he was not given residency status.

noticias.titulo: WHO chief urges end to US fuel blockade on Cuba
noticias.resumen: UN allocates $2m for immunisation and medical equipment as Cuban healthcare struggles with critical shortages.
noticias.texto:
WHO chief urges end to US fuel blockade on Cuba
UN allocates $2m for immunisation, medical equipment as Cuban healthcare struggles with critical shortages.
World Health ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has called for the lifting of a US fuel blockade on Cuba, as shortages dent the island’s once vaunted healthcare system.
Tedros warned that the sanctions were endangering the lives of children on Tuesday, during a visit to Cuba that included tours of several healthcare facilities in Havana.
“The intensification of fuel restrictions and sanctions is causing direct harm to the Cuban people, especially the most vulnerable,” Tedros said.
During his three-day visit, the United Nations health agency’s top official said his organisation would contribute $2m to help strengthen Cuba’s ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌national immunisation programme and provide essential medical equipment to healthcare facilities.
The UN has repeatedly warned of a growing humanitarian crisis on the island, calling the US blockade a violation of international law and the human rights of all Cubans.
Cuba’s government says the measures led to daily power outages lasting 20 hours or more, critical shortages of medicines and surgical supplies, and a decline in health indicators, such as infant mortality rates.
Tedros met with Cuba’s President Miguel Diaz-Canel on Tuesday to discuss the country’s health needs.
“We agreed on the need to prioritise essential health services and time-sensitive interventions, particularly for children,” Tedros wrote in a post on X.
“Fuel restrictions and sanctions affecting the purchase of medical products are severely impacting the health system that Cuban doctors have built over decades.”
Falling life expectancy
Tedros said during a news conference that Cuba’s life expectancy had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025, the first decline since records began in 1950.
The 2025 figures predate the imposition by the administration of US President Donald Trump of a fuel blockade and stiff sanctions against a ‌number of Cuban officials and entities in January.
Washington argues the energy blockade is intended to push for political change on the island and says that exports of food and medicine are subject to legal exemptions.
An annual non-binding resolution calling for an end to a US embargo on the island has ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌passed ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌in favour of Cuba in the UN General Assembly by wide margins every year since 1992.

noticias.titulo: Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
noticias.resumen: The Yashar party says it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel's Our Home party, led by Avigdor Lieberman.
noticias.texto:
Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
The Yashar party says it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party, led by Avigdor Lieberman.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has announced an agreement to unite with a right-wing opposition party in a bid to form the next Israeli government following October’s elections.
The Yashar party said on Tuesday that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
After no party managed to secure a 61-seat majority, Israel’s parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, while Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister despite the October 27 election stripping Netanyahu of his majority.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
Arab parties
The agreement between Eisenkot, whose party won 21 parliament seats, and Lieberman, whose party won seven, was unforeseen since Lieberman has been vocal about his opposition to forming a government with support from Arab parties as well as to a unity government with Netanyahu.
Lieberman had once served as foreign minister under a previous Netanyahu government but has since become a strong critic.
Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud’s alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners, including Lieberman, hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel’s Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
The path forward
Talks are also ongoing between Eisenkot, some of his “change bloc” partners and Likud on forming a unity government.
The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot after the Yashar party leader’s talks with Netanyahu’s Likud on a possible unity government.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with Arab parties.

noticias.titulo: Poll finds US voters want government to end Iran war regardless of terms
noticias.resumen: New survey finds that 55 percent of voters, including 80 percent of Democrats, want war brought to an end immediately.
noticias.texto:
Poll finds US voters want government to end Iran war regardless of terms
New survey finds that 55 percent of voters, including 80 percent of Democrats, want the Iran war brought to an end immediately.
A new poll has found that a majority of voters in the United States want an end to the US-Israel war on Iran immediately, even if it means accepting less favourable conditions.
Overall, 55 percent of those surveyed agreed with an “end to the war now, regardless of the terms”.
That number was even higher among Democrats and independents, who agreed with the statement at a rate of 80 percent and 59 percent, respectively. About 25 percent of Republicans said the same.
A majority of Democratic voters also supported steps to pressure the administration of President Donald Trump to stop the conflict.
Fifty-three percent of party members said they would favour Congress withholding funding for military operations, and 51 percent would back an “an Iran war-funding cutoff” in upcoming budget negotiations, even if the manoeuvre risked a government shutdown.
The numbers were published on Tuesday as part of the latest Critical Issues Poll, released by the University of Maryland and the research firm Ipsos.
Shibley Telhami, the poll’s principal investigator, said he was surprised by the level of support for ending the war, regardless of the terms.
“We knew that people were strongly opposed to this war and wanted it to end,” he told Al Jazeera in a phone call. “What we were less sure of is what they would be willing to accept to achieve this.”
The survey asked 1,022 US adults about their perspectives on the war.
In one question, they were tasked with assessing with three options: whether to end the conflict immediately, escalate militarily, or continue on the current path in order to extract concessions from Iran.
Just 21 percent of all respondents favoured the current path, and 18 percent supported escalation.
“Clearly, the public mood is to end it now, whatever it takes,” said Telhami.
Questioning the rationale for war
Voters also appear sceptical about the US government’s arguments in favour of the war, which include dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme.
The Critical Issues Poll found that only 28 percent of those surveyed believed that the war had left Iran in “worse position” to develop nuclear weapons.
While the US has long voiced concerned that Iran could pursue nuclear arms, intelligence assessments have not found evidence that Tehran has authorised such a step since abandoning its nuclear weapons programme in 2003.
The Strait of Hormuz has also emerged as a key issue, with Iran closing the waterway to commercial traffic early in the war. The Trump administration has responded with a naval blockade in the strait.
Some 20 percent of the world’s oil supply passes through the maritime artery, and fuel prices have spiked as a result of the war.
About 35 percent of respondents in Tuesday’s poll said that they believe Iran is now in control of the strait, while just 12.7 percent said the US is in control.
The poll comes as the Democratic Party is debating how far it should go to end the unpopular war.
In the recent midterm elections, backlash against the war — and as well as related issues like rising fuel prices — contributed to big gains for the Democratic Party.
Trump’s Republican Party, meanwhile, suffered one of its most bruising setbacks in modern US history, losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Members of the Democratic Party’s anti-war left have pointed to the results as proof that voters want an end to the war and an end to US support for Israel.
But that position has brought them into conflict with members of the party’s more hawkish establishment wing.
While leaders such as Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer have both expressed support for ending the war, they have yet to commit to aggressive strategies to reach that goal.
That includes potentially cutting off funding for military operations against Iran, or using an upcoming funding battle in December to demand that the White House end the war.
“A lot of Democratic figures are dismissing the intensity of public feeling on this issue,” said Telhami. “If they don’t adapt, they will be left behind.”
He added that progressive figures such as Senator Bernie Sanders and Senator Chris Van Hollen have been among those pressing for a more assertive stance.
Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer to lead the Democratic majority in the US Senate, has used the war to portray the party’s moderate leadership as out of step with voters.
The poll found that Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer by a ratio of nearly three to one.

noticias.titulo: Alaska ends deal to give voter records to US Justice Department
noticias.resumen: The decision follows the conclusion of the 2026 midterm elections and an effort under Trump to gather state voter rolls.
noticias.texto:
Alaska ends deal to give voter records to US Justice Department
The decision follows the conclusion of the 2026 midterm elections and an effort under Trump to collect state voter rolls.
Alaska has terminated a memorandum of understanding that granted the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) access to the state’s voter rolls.
On Monday, outgoing Lieutenant Governor Nancy Dahlstrom, who oversees the state’s elections, announced she had notified the Justice Department that Alaska was withdrawing from the 2025 memo, effective immediately.
In a statement, Dahlstrom said her state had entered the agreement “in good faith to cooperate with our federal law enforcement partners”. But she acknowledged a shift had taken place after the 2026 midterm elections.
“The circumstances have now changed,” Dahlstrom wrote. “The election has concluded and the agreement no longer serves a continuing purpose.”
The reversal comes after months of pressure from the administration of President Donald Trump for states to surrender their voter rolls to federal authorities.
Trump has argued that such information was necessary to root out fraud during the November 3 midterms.
But officials in certain states argued that the federal government was encroaching on their constitutional authority. Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections.
Experts have also called Trump’s claims of “rigged” elections unsubstantiated.
No voters flagged for removal
The memorandum, signed last December at the Justice Department’s behest, established terms under which federal officials could flag potentially ineligible voters on Alaska’s voter rolls.
“Since that time, the DOJ has not identiﬁed any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska’s voter registration records,” the state Division of Elections said.
“No voters were removed from Alaska’s voter rolls as a result of the agreement.”
The announcement came as the state certified its November 3 midterm election results, in which Democrats flipped a Senate seat and won the governor’s office.
Alaska was one of several surprise battlegrounds during the midterms.
Democrat Mary Peltola unseated two-term Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a fiercely contested Senate race marred by allegations of a spoiler candidate recruited to sabotage the senator’s re-election bid.
Meanwhile, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the state’s governorship, ending nearly three decades of Republican control in that office.
Democrats nationwide made significant gains, flipping both chambers of Congress in the midterms.
That result was largely fuelled by voter frustration under Trump, whose Republican Party suffered defeats in former strongholds like Texas.
A legal battle over voter rolls
Faced with drooping approval ratings in the lead-up to the election, Trump had falsely claimed that many non-citizens were registered to vote across the country.
His administration sued some 30 states as well as Washington, DC, after they declined to hand over their unredacted voter rolls for review.
Twenty-eight of those cases were ultimately dismissed in court, according to the Brennan Center for Justice, a public policy institute at New York University.
The Justice Department suffered a further setback last month when a federal judge struck down its nationwide voter-list maintenance programme, ruling that it lacked legal authority to collect and assess state registration lists. The administration has appealed the ruling.
Alaska was one of at least 16 states that complied with the administration’s demands for voter roll access.
But it was sued by voting rights advocates for surrendering voter information, in violation of the Alaska Constitution.
In its Monday statement, Alaska’s Division of Elections said it had directed the Justice Department to destroy Alaska’s confidential voter information in accordance with the 2025 memo — a move that could have implications for the pending lawsuit.
On Tuesday, Democratic State Senator Bill Wielechowski suggested the latest termination was timed to prevent further scrutiny from the lawsuit.
“The real reason they did this is to try to make the lawsuit over this release go away before the incoming Gov. Kreiss-Tomkins Administration could settle or produce discovery,” Wielechowski wrote on social media.
Kreiss-Tomkins is set to be sworn in as governor on December 7.
Wielechowski also noted that Alaska’s request for the Trump administration to delete the records is “likely meaningless”, since federal authorities have “undoubtedly already loaded it” onto government databases.
In its Monday statement, Alaska’s Division of Elections said its decision to end the memo did not constitute an admission of wrongdoing.
The state’s interests, it added, were “best served by terminating the agreement and continuing to rely on its established voter list-maintenance procedures”.
A Justice Department spokesperson told The Associated Press on Tuesday that the department would issue a formal response to the state.

noticias.titulo: Rebel group retreats in DR Congo after heavy clashes with government forces
noticias.resumen: CRP halts advance towards Bunia, citing commitments made during Ugandan-mediated talks with government.
noticias.texto:
Rebel group retreats in DR Congo after heavy clashes with government forces
CRP halts advance towards Bunia, citing commitments made during Ugandan-mediated talks with the government.
The rebel group led by convicted war criminal Thomas Lubanga has withdrawn from areas recently seized in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) after days of heavy fighting with government forces.
The Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) announced on Tuesday that it had decided to halt an advance towards the town of Bunia, the capital of Ituri province in northeast DRC.
In a statement, the group cited a commitment made in talks with the Congolese government, mediated by Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni, as one of the reasons for its withdrawal.
The CRP’s decision came one day after the group seized the Iga-Barriere, a strategic area about 25km north of Bunia, forcing government troops to withdraw towards the provincial capital.
Lubanga, a former leader of the Union of Congolese Patriots, was convicted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2012 on charges of recruiting and using child soldiers.
He was sentenced to 14 years in prison and released in March 2020 after completing his sentence. Lubanga remains sanctioned by the United Nations.
Lubanga announced the formation of the CRP in 2025, opening another front against the DRC’s President Felix Tshisekedi.
The group said the decision to withdraw troops was made “out of respect for the commitments made at the State House” by the Congolese government and the CRP, referring to an October 9 meeting hosted by Uganda between Lubanga and a delegation of senior government and military officials.
Disrupting Ebola response
On Sunday, the World ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Health Organization said fighting near a hospital in the Ituri province, north of Bunia, forced the evacuation of health workers and aid partners, disrupting Ebola response efforts.
The DRC is experiencing its largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak, which has spread across the country’s east and northeast. Ituri remains one of the most affected provinces.
Thousands of civilians have reportedly been displaced towards Bunia since the weekend due to renewed fighting between rebel fighters and government forces, according to local media reports.

noticias.titulo: South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to fight Ukraine for Russia
noticias.resumen: The Zimbabwean man was arrested on November 8 at a Johannesburg airport while attempting to board a flight to Russia.
noticias.texto:
South Africa convicts Zimbabwean who tried to fight Ukraine for Russia
The Zimbabwean man was arrested on November 8 at a Johannesburg airport while attempting to board a flight to Russia.
A South African court has convicted and sentenced a Zimbabwean man for trying to travel to Russia to fight in Ukraine after he was arrested earlier this month alongside eight others.
Tafadzwa Sithole was sentenced to five years in prison on Tuesday, under a five-year suspension, meaning he would only have to serve the time if he is convicted of a similar crime within that time period. Sithole is set to be deported back to Zimbabwe.
He told the court that he had agreed to fight for Russia in the war in exchange for “remuneration” after successfully applying online in Zimbabwe.
“He knew that the Russian Federation was engaged in an ongoing armed conflict with Ukraine and that the military service he intended to render would be performed in the context of that armed conflict,” his lawyer told the court.
Sithole was arrested at OR Tambo international airport on November 8 while attempting to board a flight to Russia.
Foreign Military Assistance Act
Sithole said a person he identified as “Albina” contacted him after he submitted the application, arranged accommodation in South Africa and provided a flight ticket to Russia. His admissions were detailed in a plea agreement with South African prosecutors.
He pleaded guilty to violating the Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act. The act prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training, and also applies to foreign nationals.
Sithole, who described himself as an unemployed third-year student at a university in Zimbabwe, appeared in court with four other accused who are also negotiating plea agreements with prosecutors.
He said he entered South Africa legally on November 4 and stayed in an accommodation in Kempton Park, east of Johannesburg, in preparation for his travel to Russia.
Larger issue at play
Zimbabwe is among several African countries where Russia has been recruiting fighters for its war against Ukraine. Others include South Africa, Kenya, Botswana and Ghana.
Zimbabwean authorities said in March that 15 citizens had been killed in the war in Ukraine and that they were seeking the return of 66 others. The government said recruits were promised well-paid jobs but had their travel documents confiscated and were forced into combat.
Kenya’s government said in February that more than 1,000 citizens had been recruited to fight for Russia. Families protested in Nairobi in March, demanding their relatives’ return and the prosecution of those responsible.
An investigation by Code for Africa, a nonprofit data journalism and technology organisation, identified 289 websites, domains and social media profiles used to lure recruits through false advertising and promises of generous benefits.

noticias.titulo: Arsenal and Dortmund draw 1-1 as Gyokeres goes from hero to villain
noticias.resumen: Arsenal dominate the chances as Borussia Dortmund fight back for a 1-1 draw in football's Champions League.
noticias.texto:
Arsenal and Dortmund draw 1-1 as Gyokeres goes from hero to villain
Arsenal dominate the chances as Borussia Dortmund fight back for a 1-1 draw in football’s Champions League.
Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres showed why he is such a polarising figure with a thunderous goal and a crucial miss in Tuesday’s 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League.
Gunners boss Mikel Arteta had urged Gyokeres to seize his opportunity after selecting the Swedish striker instead of Kai Havertz for the league phase tie at London’s Emirates Stadium.
Initially, Gyokeres looked like he was doing just that with his first goal at Emirates this season, and only his third for the Gunners in all competitions.
But the 28-year-old has been much maligned for his erratic displays since arriving from Sporting Lisbon in 2025.
And he gave more ammunition to his critics when he missed a golden opportunity to seal the points with a woeful header in the closing stages.
Dortmund had equalised through Maximilian Beier by then, and Arteta was left to rue his decision to put his faith in Gyokeres.
Arsenal are unbeaten in their last 11 games in all competitions, but this was not a vintage display by the English champions, who failed to win at home for the first time this season.
In a showdown between the current leaders of the Premier League and the Bundesliga, Arsenal were too profligate in attack and error-prone at the back to say they deserved all three points.
Arsenal sit fifth in the league phase with three wins and two draws from their five matches, while seventh-placed Dortmund are one point behind them.
Arteta will hope for a much more ruthless display in a significant Premier League showdown with spluttering title rivals Manchester City in north London on Sunday.
Arsenal were in control at the start, and Christos Tzolis’s strike bounced just over before Gyokeres tested Dortmund keeper Gregor Kobel with a long-range drive.
It was a warning Dortmund failed to heed as Gyokeres put Arsenal ahead in the 10th minute.
Fatally backing off when Gyokeres took possession 25 yards from goal, Dortmund’s defenders were punished by the Swede as he unleashed a superb dipping strike that flashed into the roof of the net.
Arsenal’s luck runs out in Champions League
Tzolis nearly doubled Arsenal’s lead with a curler that forced a sprawling save from Kobel.
Declan Rice almost replicated Gyokeres’s goal with a ferocious blast that fizzed just over.
Kepa Arrizabalaga was deputising for David Raya in goal for Arsenal after his fellow Spaniard suffered a shoulder injury in Saturday’s draw at Newcastle.
Such was Arsenal’s dominance that Kepa did not make a save until the final minute of the first half when he blocked Joane Gadou’s shot at the near post.
But Dortmund have a well-earned reputation as a stronger team in the second half this season, and they lived up to that tag once again.
Dortmund had a strong penalty appeal rejected after Gyokeres blocked a corner with his arm.
And with Arsenal unusually sloppy at the back, Dortmund’s pressure was rewarded in the 55th minute.
Gadou surged towards the Arsenal area before slipping a pass into Beier, who eluded Gabriel Magalhaes to plant a clinical low finish past Kepa.
Kobel saved Piero Hincapie’s close-range header as Arsenal tried to respond, while Dortmund midfielder Jobe Bellingham had a goal disallowed for a tight offside.
Gyokeres wasted his chance to finish as Arsenal’s hero for once when he sent a close-range diving header woefully wide from Martin Odegaard’s cross.
Arsenal’s luck was out after Odegaard’s delivery twice hit the post and appeared to strike Serhou Guirassy’s hand before it was finally scrambled clear.
Rice was equally unfortunate with a first-time drive that cannoned back off the near post to leave Arsenal frustrated.

noticias.titulo: India news: US prepares new tariffs after trade probe
noticias.resumen: The United States is reportedly readying fresh tariffs on India and 15 other economies under a trade probe. Also, a woman was allegedly gangraped by her colleagues in the national capital. Follow live.
noticias.texto:
India news: Trump administration set to unveil new tariffs after probe
November 25, 2026
What you need to know
- USTR set to unveil results of a probe on excess industrial capacity in India and 15 other economies
- Probe could lead to fresh tariffs on India and others
- Woman allegedly gangraped in Delhi by her colleagues
Here are the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, November 25:
US set to unveil new tariffs after probe on excess factory capacity
India could be one of the 16 countries facing fresh and imminent US tariffs with the Trump administration set to release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacities, Reuters reported citing three people with knowledge of the matter.
The results of the investigation are likely to be released over the course of the day, followed by new import duties on a wide range of goods if the probe find India guilty of excess capacity.
It remains unclear what tariff rates would be proposed but one of the sources told the news agency that they would be specifically tailored to each country.
That said, the US is likely to honor capped tariff rates agreed on in finalized US trade deals with partner countries.
A report by the Wall Street Journal said that India could face higher US tariffs than economies like Japan or the European Union.
Where are US tariffs on India?
The US introduced 25% reciprocal tariffs in 2025 on India, under US President Donald Trump's second term. The rate was later lowered to 18% with Washington and New Delhi agreeing to an interim trade framework while a more comprehensive trade agreement would be worked on. Leaders from both nations have since said the first tranche of a trade agreement was "close," but a deal remains elusive.
Meanwhile in July 2026, the United States Trade Representative (USTR), which carries out trade-related investigations, imposed an additional 10% tariffs on India and other countries after a probe on traded goods made using forced labor.
Welcome to our coverage
Good morning! and welcome to DW's India blog.
This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from Studio Delhi and I will be your guide through India's news cycle.
The national capital once again woke up to the news of an alleged gang-rape in east Delhi where a woman was assaulted by her colleagues on Monday night. Local media reports say at least one of the three held is a woman, while three others remain absconding.
In other news, India is among a bunch of countries that might face fresh US tariffs under a trade investigation. US President Donald Trump's administration has been using trade probes as a proxy to reciprocal tariffs. The results of the latest probe are expected soon.
Stay tuned for this and more.

noticias.titulo: Libya: 2 dead after Ukrainian attack on Russian warship in Benghazi
noticias.resumen: The head of the eastern administration in Libya has confirmed that two Libyan soldiers succumbed to their injures. Ukraine's foreign minister defended the attack as an effort to counter Russian aggression.
noticias.texto:
Libya: 2 dead after Ukrainian attack on Russian warship in Benghazi
November 25, 2026
Two Libyan soldiers have died from their injuries sustained during a Ukrainian attack on a Russian warship in docked in the port of Benghazi.
Libya is currently divided between a UN-recognized government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east of the country that controls Benghazi.
The head of the eastern administration, Oussama Hamad, said the two men had died "as a result of their injuries during the treacherous Ukrainian aggression against the port of Benghazi."
The Libyan National Army General Command said a response would come "at the appropriate time and place."
Earlier, on Monday, Libya's Foreign ministry denounced the attacks and said it didn't authorize "any foreign military operations within [Libya's] territory or territorial waters.
Ukraine denies dragging Libya into war
The naval drone attack that occurred on Sunday was claimed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday. On Tuesday, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha defended the attack.
"Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Sybiha said on Telegram.
"Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended ‌to harm Libya or its people."
He said Russia was the one endangering third countries by using their civilian infrastrure for military purposes.
According to the Institute for the Study of War, the Russian corvette warship had stopped for several days in Benghazi's port to refuel and resupply.
Another Ukrainian naval drone attack on Sunday sank a Russian-owned container ship that was allegedly transporting military equipment.
Ukraine has in recent months sought to attack Russian targets further and further away, including a series of strikes in Siberia.

noticias.titulo: China launches Shenzhou-24 to Tiangong station
noticias.resumen: A new Chinese crew is on its way to the Tiangong station after a launch that China called a complete success. This includes a Pakistani pilot, who is making a brief visit.
noticias.texto:
China launches Shenzhou-24 to Tiangong station
November 25, 2026
The Shenzhou-24 spacecraft lifted off on a Long March-2F rocket at 8:18 am local time (0018 GMT) from the Jiuquan launch center in the Gobi Desert.
The China Manned Space Agency reported that the capsule separated from the rocket about 10 minutes later and entered orbit, and called the launch a "complete success".
State broadcaster CCTV showed the three crew members leafing through a manual minutes after liftoff and reported that they were in good condition.
What do we know about the crew?
Tang Hongbo is making his third trip to space. CCTV said he will become the first astronaut to board Tiangong three times. Wu Yi is on his first flight, as is Pakistani pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to fly on a Chinese crewed mission.
"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.
The handover on the station will be unusual. Shenzhou-23 commander Zhu Yangzhu will remain on board for a year, while the rest of his crew — Lai Ka-ying, Hong Kong's first astronaut, and Zhang Zhiyuan — return to Earth with Ali.
Zhu's stay is reportedly China's first full-year spell in space. Reuters said it will be the longest single stay by a Chinese astronaut. It has been described as a test of how the human body copes, ahead of planned Moon missions and possibly a journey to Mars.
What is on the agenda?
The crew will carry out more than 90 experiments and technology tests, Xinhua reported. At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology had made teamwork harder, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
Ali, speaking in Mandarin, told reporters: "It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights."
China's 2030 target for a crewed Moon landing is unchanged despite the delay to its Chang'e-7 lunar mission. The United States is aiming for 2028.

noticias.titulo: US jury convicts Huawei of violating sanctions, stealing trade secrets
noticias.resumen: Huawei was found guilty of 10 out of 12 charges levelled against it. The company said it plans to appeal the verdict.
noticias.texto:
US jury convicts Huawei of violating sanctions, stealing trade secrets
November 25, 2026
A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei on a slew of charges on Tuesday including stealing trade secrets and violating sanctions.
The jury in the Brooklyn federal court found the company guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts that it faced, which also included bank fraud and wire fraud.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said after the verdict.
However, the jury acquitted Huawei on two charges of racketeering and conspiring to obstruct justice.
The verdict is the latest blow to the Chinese tech giant which has for years been banned from selling networking devices to telecom carries in the US and other Western countries. However, its consumer electronics business has continued to grow as its networking business in other countries.
Stolen source code, antenna technology and robot tech
Prosecutors detailed a number of ways Huawei stole trade secrets from competitors in order to undercut them in the market.
In once instance, a Huawei employee slipped into a competitor's booth at a Chicago trade fair in order to photograph circuitboards inside another company's networking divice.
Huawei was also found to have once sold routers containing source code from a rival company.
Prosecutors also said a Huawei employee once removed a robotic arm from a competitor's lab so it could be photographed and measured.
According to court records, the victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu.
"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the Department of Justice said.
False statenments about Iran operations
Prosecutors also alleged that Huawei did business in countries subject to US sanctions including Iran and North Korea.
Huawei then made false statements to both US government officials and banks in order to hide this activity, prosecutors said.
"Few crimes are as serious as Huawei's decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the ‌enforcement of US laws," US Attorney Joseph Nocella said.
Huawei to appeal verdict
Huawei continued to deny the allegations even after the verdict on Tuesday.
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," the company said in a statement.
"The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades. No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation."
The company's lawyer, Brian Heberlig, said: "We fully expect to appeal."
Huawei is set to be sentenced next September and could face billions of dollars in penalties.

noticias.titulo: China sends first foreign astronaut to its space station as Pakistani joins Shenzhou 24 crew
noticias.resumen: China launches Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying foreign crew
noticias.texto:
China launches Shenzhou 24 spacecraft carrying foreign crew
China has launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with a Pakistani astronaut on board, the first time a foreign national has flown to its Tiangong space station.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, lifted off on Wednesday morning with Chinese crewmates Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.
Hours earlier, crowds gathered for a send-off ceremony, many filming on their phones.
Following the launch, the capsule separated from its rocket and reached its planned orbit.
It is the first joint flight of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's crewed space programme.
Pakistanis celebrate astronaut's feat
Thousands of kilometres away, Pakistanis watched the ascent on television at home and in restaurants, chanting slogans in praise of God and of Pakistan-China friendship. Scientists at the national space agency's headquarters followed the launch live.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the mission a source of national pride and an inspiration for the country's youth.
"This is not just one astronaut's journey, but the journey of 240 million Pakistanis," he wrote on X. He thanked Beijing for including a Pakistani astronaut and said the flight extended the two countries' close ties into space.
Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, speaking to reporters at the agency, thanked President Xi Jinping, China's leadership and its scientists and engineers, and said he hoped the flight would be the start of broader cooperation.
Asked whether Pakistan could one day send astronauts on its own, he replied: "Certainly that day will come."
Iqbal said Ali carried the Pakistani flag on his uniform, lifting his compatriots' hopes and technological ambitions into orbit. "The sky is no longer our limit; it is our launching pad," he said, calling the mission an inspiration for young Pakistanis hoping for careers in science and technology.
Mission to carry out more than 90 scientific experiments
The flight stems from an agreement the two countries signed in February 2025. Xinhua reported that the crew will carry out more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests.
Ali, who is on a short-term mission, will run an experiment on photosynthetic cyanobacteria before returning to Earth aboard Shenzhou 23. Ali and Wu are making their first spaceflight. Tang has flown twice before and is set to become the first astronaut to board Tiangong three times, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
At a press conference on Tuesday, Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology had made training together harder, but that the effort was paying off.
Ali showed as much by speaking Mandarin and citing a line of Chinese poetry about climbing higher to see farther. "It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said.
Switching to English, Ali said he hoped cooperation would grow from one astronaut on one flight to multiple joint missions and eventually to the Moon, Mars and beyond.
China is preparing to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030. The United States is widely seen as its main rival, with NASA aiming to put astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

noticias.titulo: Summer vitamin D levels may say more about your health than winter levels, study finds
noticias.resumen: A Swedish research team set out to identify who could benefit most from taking vitamin D supplements.
noticias.texto:
A Swedish research team set out to identify who could benefit most from taking vitamin D supplements.
Low vitamin D in the summertime may be a bigger red flag for your health than in the winter months, a new study has found.
Vitamin D helps the body regulate calcium and phosphate in the body, keeping our bones, teeth and muscles healthy. Most of it comes from sunlight, while people can also get some vitamin D from foods such as oily fish, eggs and some mushrooms. Millions of Europeans also take vitamin D supplements, though randomised trials have largely failed to show that routine supplementation improves health or boosts longevity.
Researchers from Uppsala University in Sweden wondered if seasonal swings in vitamin D levels might help explain why. In Europe and much of the Northern Hemisphere, people build up stores of vitamin D in their fat during the sunny summer months, and they may draw on those reserves as their vitamin D levels naturally fall in the darker winter months.
“We need to better understand who truly needs vitamin D supplementation,” the researchers wrote.
To find out, the researchers analysed vitamin D levels in the blood of more than 12,000 older people in Sweden. They split participants into groups based on whether their blood was drawn in summer, from July to September, or in winter, from January to March.
People with low vitamin D levels in summer were more likely to fracture a bone or die over the next 11 years, on average, than those with high summer levels. Meanwhile, people who had low vitamin D levels in the winter months were not at increased risk of bone fracture or death, according to the study, which was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.
People were considered to have low vitamin D if their blood concentration was below 40 nanomoles per litre (nmo/L) and high levels if it was above 80 nmol/L.
The findings suggest summer could be the best time to test vitamin D levels. That could help doctors identify people who are chronically low and could benefit the most from supplements, the researchers said.
“We should think carefully about when we measure vitamin D,” the researchers wrote. “Winter measurements are heavily influenced by seasonal variation, whereas low vitamin D levels during summer are more likely to reflect persistently low vitamin D status and a higher risk of adverse health outcomes.”
This was an observational study, meaning it cannot show whether low vitamin D levels cause bone fractures or early death. It was also conducted mainly in white Swedish people, so the results may not directly apply to other groups. Still, the findings held even after the researchers accounted for age, sex, body size and other factors.
The researchers said more randomised trials are needed to identify the potential health benefits of supplements, ideally focused on people with low vitamin D levels in the summer.

noticias.titulo: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat and orders Bern's new Pyongyang office to close
noticias.resumen: Switzerland opened the office on 19 October, when Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis travelled to Pyongyang and met senior officials, including his counterpart Choe Son Hui.
noticias.texto:
Switzerland opened the office on 19 October, when Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis travelled to Pyongyang and met senior officials, including his counterpart Choe Son Hui.
North Korea has ordered Switzerland to shut its newly opened diplomatic office in Pyongyang and given its head 48 hours to leave the country in retaliation for Swiss sanctions on a children's camp linked to Russia.
State news agency KCNA reported on Wednesday that a senior Foreign Ministry official called in Astier Sylvain, who leads the Swiss mission, and handed him a written demand for the office's closure. Pyongyang declared him persona non grata.
The move follows a warning on Tuesday from Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un and one of the regime's leading foreign policy voices, who called the sanctions an "open hostile act" that violated North Korean sovereignty.
The expulsion comes five weeks after Benn restarted operations in Pyongyang.
A rare Western channel under strain
Switzerland opened the office on 19 October, when Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis travelled to Pyongyang and met senior officials, including his counterpart Choe Son Hui.
KCNA said the talks covered "promoting dialogue and cooperation." The office reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing, and Bern said it would help build direct contact with North Korean officials.
Switzerland has had diplomatic relations with North Korea since 1974 and remains one of the few Western states to keep a line open. Its development agency ran a cooperation office in Pyongyang from 1997, focused largely on humanitarian work, until it closed in March 2020, when North Korea sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The Swiss Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday that it wanted to keep channels of dialogue open despite political differences.
It stressed that reopening the office is separate from its sanctions policy, whether UN measures tied to North Korea's nuclear programme or the EU sanctions Switzerland has adopted over Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The camp at the centre of the dispute
Bern recently added the Songdowon International Children's Camp, in the coastal city of Wonsan, to its sanctions list over Russia's war in Ukraine.
Swiss authorities say the facility is part of programmes that bring Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territory to North Korea, where they are exposed to pro-Russian propaganda.
The UK sanctioned the camp in May, and the EU followed in September, freezing its assets and banning financial dealings with it. Given North Korea's minimal financial links with Europe, the practical effect of these measures is uncertain.
Kim Yo Jong said the camp serves "legitimate" cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. She did not directly respond to Western allegations that abducted Ukrainian children have been sent there for re-education.
North Korea has moved steadily closer to Russia during the war, supplying thousands of troops and large quantities of weapons to support Vladimir Putin's invasion, possibly in return for aid and military technology.
Closer relations with Moscow and Beijing have underpinned Kim Jong Un's more assertive foreign policy as he seeks to end the country's isolation and present it as part of a bloc opposed to Washington.
